items.stem: Since retiring from competitive climbing, Bo runs a small guiding service taking clients up the routes he loves, working only the seasons he chooses and employing one part-time assistant. The service uses standard equipment and methods, brings in a comfortable income, and Bo has no interest in expanding it. In the chapter's typology, Bo is running:
options: A lifestyle firm
A salary-substitute firm
An entrepreneurial firm
A conservative firm
rationales: Correct — lifestyle firms give their owners the chance to pursue a particular sport, hobby, or pastime while earning a living at it; they are not innovative, do not grow quickly, and often employ only the owner or a handful of people. Guides are among the chapter's own examples, and Bo's service is organized around the climbing and the seasons, not around growth or novelty.

A salary-substitute firm is defined by yielding ordinary-job-level income from a common, easily available service; what defines Bo's service is the way of living it is built around, not paycheck replacement.
Entrepreneurial firms bring new products and services to market; Bo uses standard equipment and methods and has no interest in growth.
Conservative describes an established firm's wait-and-see position on the entrepreneurial continuum — it is not one of the chapter's three start-up types.
probes: Is the service defined by replacing a paycheck, or by the way of living it is built around?
Is Bo bringing anything new to market, or offering a standard service on his own terms?
Is 'conservative' one of the chapter's three start-up types, or a point on a different continuum?

items.stem: After her position at a distribution warehouse was eliminated, Ines used her savings to open a neighborhood dry-cleaning shop. It offers the same services at the same prices as the other cleaners in town, and it brings in about what her old job paid. She wants steady income, not expansion. In the chapter's typology, Ines is running:
options: A salary-substitute firm
A lifestyle company
An entrepreneurial firm
A conservative firm
rationales: Correct — salary-substitute firms are small firms that yield their owners a level of income similar to what they would earn working for an employer, offering common, easily available, and not particularly innovative products or services. Dry cleaners are one of the chapter's own examples, and Ines's shop matches the description on every point.
Lifestyle firms are organized around a sport, hobby, or pastime the owner wants to live; nothing marks dry cleaning as that for Ines — the shop exists to replace her lost paycheck.
Entrepreneurial firms bring new products and services to market; Ines's services are identical to her competitors', which is precisely what her shop does not do.
Conservative names a wait-and-see behavioral posture on the entrepreneurial continuum for existing firms — it is not one of the three start-up types.
probes: Is dry cleaning presented here as a way of living Ines wants, or as a way to replace her paycheck?
What would the shop need to bring to market for the chapter to call it entrepreneurial?
Is 'conservative firm' one of the three start-up types the chapter lists?

items.stem: Amara founds a company around a sensor-equipped bandage she developed that alerts nurses remotely when a wound shows early signs of infection — something no existing product does. Hospitals adopt it quickly because it prevents complications and saves staff time, and Amara reinvests the proceeds to reach new regions. In the chapter's typology, Amara is running:
options: An entrepreneurial firm
A salary-substitute firm
A lifestyle company
A conservative firm
rationales: Correct — entrepreneurial firms bring new products and services to market by creating and then seizing opportunities, giving customers worth, importance, and utility they would not otherwise have. The bandage is new to the market, hospitals plainly find it useful, and the firm is growing — the type's defining pattern.
Salary-substitute firms offer common, easily available services yielding job-like income; a first-of-its-kind product and reinvested growth do not fit that description.
Lifestyle firms revolve around a pastime and do not grow quickly; this company revolves around getting something new to customers and is expanding.
Conservative firms take a wait-and-see posture on the entrepreneurial continuum — a behavioral position of existing firms, not a start-up type, and Amara's company is the innovator here in any case.
probes: Does the chapter sort start-ups by where the founder's income comes from, or by what the firm brings to market?
Is this company organized around a way of living, or around getting something new to customers?
Is 'conservative' one of the three start-up types the chapter lists?

items.stem: At 63, Ruth was let go when her employer merged with a competitor. After thirty years managing supply contracts, with retirement savings she could draw on and her health intact, she is weighing a consulting practice — partly because she wants income to help cover future health-care costs. She asks a counselor at a small-business center whether launching a firm at her age makes sense. Which reply best reflects the chapter?
options: Founders her age are increasingly common and often well positioned
Founders her age are increasingly rare because most prefer retirement
Founders her age usually run their firms as pastimes rather than for income
Founders her age usually struggle because long experience transfers poorly
rationales: Correct — the chapter reports that the share of people 62 and older starting businesses has risen, driven by corporate downsizing, a desire for personal fulfillment, and worries about paying for future health care and other expenses. It adds that many people 60 and older have substantial business experience, financial resources, and good health — making them ideal candidates to start firms. Ruth's situation matches the pattern point for point.
The trend runs the other way: the SBA data the chapter cites show senior start-up activity growing, and the SBA calls that growth healthy for the economy.
The chapter lists earning additional income for future expenses, health care included, among seniors' actual motives — the financial motive has not faded.
The chapter treats seniors' decades of business experience as an asset making them ideal candidates in many industries, and investors prize experience, reputation, and track record.
probes: Which direction does the chapter say the senior start-up rate has moved?
What motives does the chapter actually list behind seniors' launches — leisure, or fulfillment and income?
Does the chapter treat decades of experience as a handicap for founders, or as an asset investors value?

items.stem: Jalen, 24, follows start-up news avidly, says entrepreneurs are the people he most admires, and has sketched several business concepts — yet he keeps accepting corporate offers, citing student loans, thin savings, and worry about what happens if a venture goes under. According to the chapter, Jalen's pattern is:
options: Typical for his age group
Unusual for his age group
A sign of insincere interest
A sign of absent role models
rationales: Correct — the chapter reports that millennials express high interest in entrepreneurship (66 percent want to start a business in the survey it cites) while a surprisingly low share actually launch: only 3.6 percent of U.S. businesses were owned by someone under 30. The cited obstacles — lack of finances, fear of failure, lack of start-up knowledge, student debt, risk aversion — are Jalen's exact profile.

The pattern is not unusual: the cited surveys show most millennials interested in founding, while people under 30 own only about 3.6 percent of U.S. businesses — his generation is not launching at a high rate.
The chapter takes the expressed interest seriously — two-thirds of millennials in the survey it cites want to start a business — and explains the gap through concrete obstacles, not insincerity.

Missing role models are not the barrier the research names; the cited obstacles are lack of finances, lack of desire, fear of failure, and lack of knowledge of the start-up process, with student debt and risk aversion among other factors.
probes: What share of U.S. businesses does the chapter say people under 30 own — and how does that compare with millennials' expressed interest?
Does the chapter read the launch gap as missing desire, or desire blocked by obstacles?
Which barriers does the chapter's cited research actually list?

items.stem: Kofi's start-up introduces an inexpensive home water-testing kit so accurate that, within a few years, households and landlords stop paying for the established mail-in laboratory services that once dominated the market. Demand for testing overall rises sharply, and the old labs either modernize or close. Which concept from the chapter does this sequence illustrate?
options: Creative destruction
Corporate entrepreneurship
Execution intelligence
A triggering event
rationales: Correct — creative destruction is Schumpeter's term for entrepreneurs developing new products and technologies that over time make current ones obsolete; because the new versions are typically better, their availability increases demand and stimulates economic activity. The labs' fate and the surge in overall testing demand are that process end to end.

Corporate entrepreneurship is an established firm behaving proactively, innovatively, and with appetite for calculated risk; the scenario's driver is a start-up displacing incumbents from outside, not an incumbent's internal orientation.
Execution intelligence is a founder's ability to fashion an idea into a viable business; the question asks about the market-level displacement the product caused, not how Kofi built his company.
A triggering event is the circumstance that prompts a person's decision to become an entrepreneur; nothing in the scenario concerns why Kofi started.
probes: Is this about what happens inside an established firm, or about what a newcomer's product does to existing ones in the market?
Are you asked how Kofi built his company, or what his product did to the incumbent labs?
Does the scenario turn on why Kofi became an entrepreneur, or on the effect his product had?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → The Positive Effects of Entrepreneurship and Entrepreneurial Firms

items.stem: Selma's start-up sells an automated customs-paperwork service that exporters plug into their shipping operations. Nearly all of her customers are corporations many times her company's size, and they subscribe because the service roughly halves what they spend processing each shipment. The chapter would cite Selma's company as an example of entrepreneurial firms':
options: Impact on larger firms
Impact on job creation
Impact on society at large
Impact on innovation
rationales: Correct — the chapter says many entrepreneurial firms build their entire business models around producing products and services that increase the efficiency or effectiveness of larger firms, citing SpeakLike's low-cost translation service and Box's cloud storage for Fortune 500 clients. Selma's cost-halving service for big exporters is that same pattern.
Job creation concerns small and young firms adding net new jobs to the economy; the scenario says nothing about hiring — its effect is on the customers' costs.

The societal impact the chapter describes is innovations improving everyday life, health, and productivity for people broadly, along with the ethical questions they raise; this is a business-to-business efficiency story.
The innovation discussion turns on patent productivity — small firms out-patenting large ones per employee; the scenario shows a service improving customers' operations, not patent activity.
probes: Whose payrolls grow in this scenario — or does the effect show up in the customers' costs instead?
Is the scenario about products changing everyday life for people broadly, or about a service sold to corporate customers?
Does anything here involve patents, or the service's effect on its customers' operations?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Entrepreneurial Firms' Impact on Larger Firms

items.stem: A state economic-development board wants its limited support budget to generate the most new jobs. Staff have profiled thousands of firms by size, age, location, and industry, and the board must pick the single firm characteristic that will drive who gets help. According to the research cited in the chapter, which characteristic is the best guide to a firm's net new job creation?
options: The firm's age
The firm's size
The firm's location
The firm's industry
rationales: Correct — the Kauffman Foundation study the chapter cites found that it is not the size of a business that matters as much as its age: companies less than one year old have created an average of 1.5 million jobs per year over the past 30 years, and new and young companies also inject competition into markets and spur innovation.
Small firms (under 500 employees) do create most net new jobs in the SBA figures, but the Kauffman study sharpens the point: age, not size, is the stronger predictor.
The chapter's job-creation evidence compares size and age; it makes no claim that employment gains concentrate in particular locations.
The chapter attributes small and young firms' job creation to effective capital deployment and market dynamism generally, not to any single industry.
probes: The SBA numbers favor small firms — but what did the Kauffman study say matters even more than size?
Does the chapter's job-creation evidence discuss geography at all?
Does the chapter confine young firms' job creation to any particular sector?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Economic Impact of Entrepreneurial Firms

items.stem: Hannah had thought about opening a bakery for years without acting. Then a modest inheritance from her aunt arrived — enough, for the first time, to cover the ovens and the first year's rent — and within a month she had committed to launching the business. In the chapter's model of the entrepreneurial process, the inheritance functions as:
options: A triggering event
A feasibility analysis
A business model
A written business plan
rationales: Correct — the chapter says a triggering event usually prompts an individual's decision to become an entrepreneur: losing a job, a lifestyle change, or receiving an inheritance that for the first time supplies the money to start a company. Hannah's inheritance is the chapter's own example of such a circumstance.
A feasibility analysis is the way to determine whether an idea represents a viable business opportunity — the money tested nothing about the bakery's viability; it changed Hannah's circumstances.
A business model is a firm's plan or recipe for how it creates, delivers, and captures value; a windfall is not a plan for the business.

A business plan is a written document that describes all aspects of a business venture in a concise manner — usually needed to raise money and attract partners; Hannah has written nothing, and the inheritance is a circumstance, not a document.
probes: Did the inheritance evaluate the bakery idea, or change Hannah's circumstances so she could act?
Is the inheritance a plan for how the bakery will create and capture value, or something that happened to Hannah?
Is the inheritance a written document describing the venture, or a change in Hannah's circumstances?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Decision to Become an Entrepreneur (Chapter 1)

items.stem: Diego never planned to run a company. But while volunteering at an animal shelter he noticed adopters constantly struggling to find pet-friendly rentals, and a matching service he sketched out gripped him so strongly that he decided, for the first time in his life, to start a firm. Which statement accurately describes how the chapter's four-step model of the entrepreneurial process handles paths like Diego's?
options: The model's first two steps connect in both directions
The model places idea development before the decision for everyone
The model imposes no order on any of its four steps
The model runs strictly one way from the decision to idea development
rationales: Correct — the model draws a double-headed arrow between the decision to become an entrepreneur and developing successful business ideas, indicating that sometimes the opportunity to develop an idea is what prompts a person to become an entrepreneur. Diego's sequence — the service concept arriving before any intention to found — is exactly the case that arrow represents.
The two-way arrow means an idea sometimes precedes the decision, not that it always does; the model's baseline still runs from deciding to become an entrepreneur toward developing ideas.
Only the first two elements are linked in both directions; the four stages otherwise proceed in order, from ideas through launching to managing and growing the firm.
The chapter singles out the arrow between the model's first two elements as double-headed — precisely so that paths like Diego's fit inside the model rather than outside it.
probes: Does the chapter say an idea always comes first, or that it sometimes prompts the decision?
Does the chapter show every step as reorderable, or a two-way link between just two of them?
Is the arrow between the model's first two elements one-way or double-headed?

items.stem: According to the chapter, which pairing correctly contrasts entrepreneurial firms with conservative firms?
options: Entrepreneurial firms are proactive innovators taking calculated risks; conservative firms wait, watch, and avoid risk
Entrepreneurial firms are defined by rapid hiring and revenue growth; conservative firms by stable payrolls and profits
Entrepreneurial firms operate mainly in technology industries; conservative firms in retail, services, and manufacturing
Entrepreneurial firms are always newly founded start-up companies; conservative firms are always decades-old businesses
rationales: Correct — the chapter describes entrepreneurial firms as proactive innovators not averse to taking calculated risks, and conservative firms as taking a wait-and-see posture, being less innovative, and being risk averse.
Growth and payroll patterns are not the chapter's contrast — the distinction is behavioral: proactiveness, innovation, and risk posture.
The chapter ties entrepreneurial behavior to no particular industry; its example of high entrepreneurial intensity is a conglomerate spanning airlines and music.
Age is not the divider — the chapter says all firms, including long-established ones, fall along the conservative-to-entrepreneurial continuum.
probes: Does the chapter contrast the two kinds of firms by financial results, or by how they behave toward innovation and risk?
Does the chapter restrict entrepreneurial firms to any particular industry?
Can an old, established firm be entrepreneurial in the chapter's account — what does the continuum apply to?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → What Is Entrepreneurship and Why Is It Important?

items.stem: Which statement best summarizes the changing demographics of U.S. entrepreneurs described in the chapter?
options: Women, minorities, and seniors own a growing number of firms, while millennials' high interest hasn't meant high participation
Women, minorities, and seniors own a shrinking share of businesses, while millennials now launch the majority of new American firms
Ownership rates have stayed flat across every demographic group, while total business formation has declined for a decade
Ownership gains are confined to technology founders in large cities, while rural and service businesses have disappeared
rationales: Correct — the chapter reports women, minorities, and seniors owning increasingly larger numbers of U.S. businesses, and flags millennials as an area of concern: high expressed interest but a surprisingly low rate of choosing the entrepreneurial path.
The chapter reports growth, not decline, for women-, minority-, and senior-owned firms — and only a small share of businesses are owned by people under 30.
The chapter documents substantial change — for example, women-owned firms grew about five times faster than the national average — not flat rates.
The chapter says women-owned firms are found in every sector of the U.S. economy, with the largest concentrations in services and health care, not technology alone.
probes: Which direction does the chapter say women-, minority-, and senior-owned business counts are moving?
Does the chapter describe the demographic makeup of entrepreneurs as static, or as changing?
Does the chapter confine the growth of women-owned firms to any one sector?

items.stem: In the chapter's account of Joseph Schumpeter's argument, why does creative destruction stimulate economic activity?
options: New products are typically better than the ones they replace, and their availability increases consumer demand
Old products and technologies keep their value indefinitely, so each innovation adds to the existing economic stock
Failed firms release workers and capital, and this recycling of resources is itself the main engine of the stimulus
Governments respond to disruptive innovation with spending programs, and that public investment drives the activity
rationales: Correct — Schumpeter, as the chapter presents him, argued that entrepreneurs' new products and technologies make current ones obsolete; because the new ones are typically better, their availability increases consumer demand and stimulates economic activity.
Creative destruction means older products are made obsolete — displaced, not preserved as accumulating stock.
The chapter's mechanism is better products raising demand and productivity, not the recycling of failed firms' resources.
Government spending appears nowhere in the chapter's account of Schumpeter — the stimulus comes from improved products and rising demand.
probes: What does creative destruction do to current products and technologies?
In the chapter's telling, what raises demand — resources being freed up, or better products becoming available?
Whose actions drive creative destruction in Schumpeter's account — entrepreneurs' or governments'?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → The Positive Effects of Entrepreneurship and Entrepreneurial Firms

items.stem: Arrange the four elements of the entrepreneurial process in the order the chapter presents them.
options: Deciding to become an entrepreneur
Developing successful business ideas
Moving from an idea to establishing an entrepreneurial firm
Managing and growing an entrepreneurial firm
rationales: Step 1 — the decision to become an entrepreneur, usually prompted by a triggering event.
Step 2 — developing successful business ideas: opportunity recognition, feasibility analysis, the business model, industry analysis, and the business plan.
Step 3 — moving from an idea to a firm: the ethical and legal foundation, financial viability, the new-venture team, and financing or funding.
Step 4 — managing and growing the firm: marketing, intellectual property, the challenges and strategies of growth, and franchising.
probes: A firm can't be established before its idea is developed — which element does the chapter's model list first, and which comes last?

items.stem: According to the chapter's model, which activities belong to the 'moving from an idea to an entrepreneurial firm' element of the entrepreneurial process?
options: Preparing the ethical and legal foundation, assessing financial strength, building the team, getting funding
Recognizing the opportunity, testing feasibility, designing the business model, writing the full business plan
Handling unique marketing issues, protecting intellectual property, and preparing for challenges of growth
Experiencing a triggering event, weighing reasons to launch, and committing to an entrepreneurial career
rationales: Correct — the chapter assigns exactly these to the third element: preparing a proper ethical and legal foundation, assessing financial strength and viability, building a new-venture team, and getting financing or funding.
These are the components of the second element, developing successful business ideas.
These belong to the fourth element, managing and growing an entrepreneurial firm.
These describe the first element, the decision to become an entrepreneur.
probes: Are those activities about establishing the firm, or about developing and vetting the idea beforehand?
Do marketing, intellectual property, and growth come while establishing the firm, or after it exists and must be managed?
Is deciding to become an entrepreneur the same element as turning an idea into a firm?

items.stem: The chapter maps its recurring features to specific employability skills. Working through the 'What Went Wrong?' features and their closing questions is chiefly meant to develop which skill?
options: Critical thinking, by pushing readers to analyze entrepreneurs' ineffective actions
Collaboration, by showing how entrepreneurs accomplish more through partnerships
Data literacy, by teaching readers to gather and interpret data about competitors
Business ethics, by explaining how firms build cultures generating ethical behavior
rationales: Correct — the chapter links critical thinking to the 'What Went Wrong?' features, whose closing questions challenge readers to think critically about what the entrepreneur could have done to avoid the mistakes that were made.
Collaboration is tied to the 'Partnering for Success' features, not to 'What Went Wrong?'.
Data literacy is developed particularly through Chapter 5's material on gathering and interpreting competitor data.
Business ethics and social responsibility are connected to Chapter 7's coverage of building an ethical culture.
probes: Which recurring feature does the chapter pair with collaboration?
Which chapter does the book link to accessing and interpreting data?
Which chapter does the book link to ethical cultures — and is that the feature named here?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Developing Skills for Your Career

items.stem: True or False: According to the chapter, studying entrepreneurship builds employability skills only for readers who intend to launch their own ventures.
options: True
False
rationales: The chapter addresses three types of readers — including those who never expect to found a firm — and says the book's contents build employability skills for all of them.

Correct — the chapter says that for all three types of readers, including those who may never become entrepreneurs, the book addresses employability skills critical to personal success within organizational settings.
probes: The chapter names three types of readers — does it say the employability skills apply to only one of them?
justify_options: Ethics, critical thinking, collaboration, and data literacy apply in any organization a reader joins
Employability skills matter only after a venture has been launched and begins hiring its employees
The chapter recommends that every reader eventually start a firm, which makes the distinction moot
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Developing Skills for Your Career

items.stem: The chapter lists data literacy among the employability skills that studying entrepreneurship develops. How does it describe what this skill lets a person do?
options: Gather information about competitors and interpret it to decide how to outperform them
Automate a firm's bookkeeping so its financial statements need no outside accountant
Secure the firm's databases so its customer records are protected from outside breaches
Forecast broad economic trends precisely enough to time a new venture's market launch
rationales: Data literacy, in the chapter, is accessing and interpreting data — for example, gathering competitor data and using it to identify ways to outperform rivals.
The chapter ties data literacy to accessing and interpreting data, not to automating a firm's accounting.
Protecting records is data security; the chapter's data literacy is about accessing and interpreting data, such as competitor data.
The chapter's example is competitor data used to outperform rivals, not forecasting the broader economy or timing a launch.
probes: Does the chapter link data literacy to accounting software, or to accessing and interpreting data?
Is safeguarding records the same as the accessing-and-interpreting skill the chapter describes?
What data did the chapter say firms gather and use — competitor data, or macroeconomic forecasts?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Developing Skills for Your Career

items.stem: Under 'Business Ethics and Social Responsibility,' the chapter says the insights a reader gains transfer beyond start-ups. What is its central claim?
options: Learning to build a culture that generates ethical employee behavior applies in any workplace
Ethical lapses rarely occur in start-ups because founders personally vet every single new hire
Social responsibility is a concern mainly for large firms that can absorb its added costs
A firm's ethics come chiefly from outside regulation, so its own culture matters little
rationales: The chapter says you learn to establish a culture that generates ethical behavior from employees — insights usable in any for-profit or not-for-profit organization, not only a venture.
The chapter doesn't say start-ups rarely have ethical lapses or that founders vet everyone; it emphasizes building an ethical culture.
The chapter says societies increasingly expect all organizations to be socially responsible, not that it is mainly for large firms.
The chapter locates ethical behavior in a strong organizational culture the firm builds, not chiefly in external regulation.
probes: Does the chapter credit ethical behavior to founder vetting, or to building an ethical culture?
Did the chapter limit social responsibility to large firms, or extend it to organizations generally?
Where does the chapter locate the source of ethics — external regulation, or the firm's own culture?
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Developing Skills for Your Career

question_sets.label: The three reasons people become entrepreneurs (LO 1.2)
question_sets.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Why Do People Become Entrepreneurs?

shared_options.theme: independence and being one's own boss
shared_options.correction: the first and most commonly given of the chapter's three reasons — usually a long-time ambition to own a firm or frustration with traditional jobs, not trouble accepting authority

shared_options.theme: seeing one's own ideas realized
shared_options.correction: the second of the chapter's three reasons — when established firms resist innovation, some employees leave to develop their ideas through a business of their own

shared_options.theme: the financial payoff of owning a firm
shared_options.correction: the third of the chapter's three reasons — typically secondary, since the average entrepreneur does not out-earn a comparable traditional job; the real lure is upside potential

shared_options.theme: starting a business because income is needed and good jobs are scarce
shared_options.correction: not one of the chapter's three primary reasons — the GEM study finds most people are drawn to entrepreneurship by attractive opportunities, with opportunity-driven founders outnumbering necessity-driven ones 3.4 to 1 in innovation-strong countries

shared_options.theme: seeking fame and public attention
shared_options.correction: not one of the chapter's three primary reasons — the chapter notes most entrepreneurs do not attract public attention, and many actively avoid it

questions.focus: the desire for independence and being one's own boss
questions.stem: Miguel has wanted to run his own company since he was a teenager; after years of reporting to three layers of managers, he finally quits his corporate job and opens his own firm. Which reason for becoming an entrepreneur does this illustrate?
questions.key_rationale: Miguel shows both drivers the chapter ties to this reason — a long-time ambition to own his own firm and frustration with a traditional corporate job — and being one's own boss is the most commonly given reason for becoming an entrepreneur.

questions.focus: wanting to see one's own idea realized
questions.stem: An engineer repeatedly proposes a new service to her employer, which declines to pursue it; convinced the idea can support a business, she leaves to develop it herself. Which reason for becoming an entrepreneur does this illustrate?
questions.key_rationale: The chapter explains that established firms often resist innovation, leaving employees with good ideas unfulfilled — and that some, out of passion and commitment, leave to start their own business as the means to develop their own ideas.

questions.focus: the financial upside of building a valuable firm
questions.stem: Dario concedes that most founders earn no more than salaried managers, but he launches a start-up anyway because, if the company's value grows, the potential payoff is enormous. Which reason for becoming an entrepreneur does this illustrate?
questions.key_rationale: The chapter notes the financial lure of entrepreneurship is its upside potential: the average entrepreneur earns no more than someone with similar responsibility in a traditional job, but building a valuable company can pay off enormously, as it did for founders like Jeff Bezos.

question_sets.label: The four characteristics of successful entrepreneurs (LO 1.3)

shared_options.theme: deep enthusiasm for the business and its idea
shared_options.correction: the chapter's number-one characteristic — passion for an idea gets a business going and keeps it going when times are tough, though it must pair with skills and a legitimate opportunity

shared_options.theme: keeping products and customers at the center
shared_options.correction: one of the four characteristics — the chapter calls products and customers the two most important elements in any business; other functions matter only if the products satisfy customers

shared_options.theme: persevering through setbacks and failures
shared_options.correction: one of the four characteristics — new ventures involve experimentation, and the chapter's litmus test for entrepreneurs is the ability to persevere through setbacks and failures

shared_options.theme: turning an idea into action and measurable results
shared_options.correction: one of the four characteristics — execution intelligence is fashioning a solid idea into a viable business through a business model, a team, funding, and partnerships

shared_options.theme: an appetite for big, high-stakes risks
shared_options.correction: not one of the four characteristics — the chapter says entrepreneurs are usually moderate risk takers, and most small-business owners rate themselves conservative rather than risky

shared_options.theme: personally inventing something new
shared_options.correction: not one of the four characteristics — the chapter distinguishes inventors, who create something new, from entrepreneurs, who assemble the resources to turn an invention into a viable business

questions.focus: deep enthusiasm for the business and its idea
questions.stem: Asked what got her fitness-equipment company started and what sustains it, Rosa answers that she believes deeply there is a better way to train — that belief inspired the product and is what keeps her going. Which characteristic of successful entrepreneurs does this show?
questions.key_rationale: Rosa echoes the chapter's number-one characteristic: passion for an idea is what gets a business going and keeps it going — like the founder of Titin, who said his passion that there is a better way to train inspired the product and keeps him going.

questions.focus: putting products and customers ahead of every other business function
questions.stem: Reviewing his start-up's priorities, Malik tells the team that finance, marketing, and management all matter — but none of it makes any difference if the firm doesn't offer good products that can satisfy customers. Which characteristic of successful entrepreneurs does this show?
questions.key_rationale: The chapter identifies products and customers as the two most important elements in any business: management, marketing, and finance make no difference unless the firm has good products with the capability to satisfy customers — the philosophy voiced by Steve Jobs and WhitePages.com's founder.

questions.focus: persevering when a venture suffers setbacks and failures
questions.stem: Customers reject the original plan behind Theo's start-up, and complaints pile up. Rather than shut down, he keeps the company alive, revises the plan around the one part that worked, and relaunches. Which characteristic of successful entrepreneurs does this show?
questions.key_rationale: The chapter's litmus test for entrepreneurs is the ability to persevere through setbacks and failures — as Yelp's founders did when their original email-recommendation plan failed and they kept the company alive and pivoted to user-written reviews rather than letting it die.

questions.focus: translating an idea into an operating, viable business
questions.stem: Nadia's meal-kit idea is hardly novel, but she methodically develops the business model, recruits a capable team, raises money, negotiates supplier partnerships, and manages the finances — turning the idea into a profitable firm. Which characteristic of successful entrepreneurs does this show?
questions.key_rationale: This is execution intelligence — the ability to fashion a solid idea into a viable business by developing a business model, putting together a new venture team, raising money, establishing partnerships, and managing finances. As the chapter quotes Jeff Bezos: ideas are easy; it's execution that's hard.

question_sets.label: The five common myths about entrepreneurs (LO 1.4)

shared_options.text: Entrepreneurs are born rather than made
shared_options.theme: whether entrepreneurial ability is inborn or developed
shared_options.correction: the chapter's Myth 1 — hundreds of studies find entrepreneurs are not genetically different from other people; becoming one is a function of environment, life experiences, and personal choices

shared_options.text: Entrepreneurs are gamblers who take big risks
shared_options.theme: risk appetite and reckless gambling
shared_options.correction: the chapter's Myth 2 — entrepreneurs are usually moderate risk takers, like most people; in one study, 79 percent of small-business owners rated themselves conservative rather than risky

shared_options.text: Entrepreneurs are motivated primarily by money
shared_options.theme: what motivates entrepreneurs
shared_options.correction: the chapter's Myth 3 — money is rarely the primary reason entrepreneurs start new firms and persevere, and some founders warn that fixating on money is distracting

shared_options.text: Entrepreneurs should be young and energetic
shared_options.theme: the age and energy of entrepreneurs
shared_options.correction: the chapter's Myth 4 — entrepreneurial activity is spread fairly evenly across age ranges, and four of the five qualities investors value in a strong entrepreneur favor older founders

shared_options.text: Entrepreneurs love the spotlight and attention
shared_options.theme: seeking fame and public attention
shared_options.correction: the chapter's Myth 5 — the vast majority of entrepreneurs do not attract public attention, and many working on proprietary products actively avoid it

shared_options.text: Entrepreneurs must invent their own products
shared_options.theme: inventing versus commercializing ideas
shared_options.correction: not one of the chapter's five myths — the chapter separately distinguishes inventors, who create something new, from entrepreneurs, who assemble the resources to turn an invention into a viable business

shared_options.theme: how often new businesses fail
shared_options.correction: not one of the chapter's five myths, though the chapter corrects it too — over half of U.S. businesses started are still in existence five years later, so the '9 out of 10 fail' figure is an exaggeration

questions.focus: whether entrepreneurial ability is inborn or developed
questions.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Myth 1: Entrepreneurs Are Born, Not Made
questions.stem: Watching a profile of successful founders, Kellan concludes that entrepreneurship must run in the blood — either you have the inborn knack or you don't, and no amount of learning can change that. Which myth is Kellan repeating?
questions.key_rationale: Kellan treats entrepreneurial ability as genetic and fixed — Myth 1. The chapter reports that hundreds of studies find entrepreneurs are not genetically different from other people; whether someone becomes one is a function of environment, life experiences, and personal choices.

questions.focus: how entrepreneurs actually approach risk
questions.stem: A business columnist writes that founders are a breed apart because they thrive on wagering everything they own on long-shot ventures. Which myth does the column reflect?
questions.key_rationale: Casting founders as high-stakes gamblers is Myth 2. The chapter says entrepreneurs are usually moderate risk takers, like most people — in The Hartford's small-business study, 79 percent of participants rated themselves conservative rather than risky.

questions.focus: what actually motivates entrepreneurs
questions.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Myth 3: Entrepreneurs Are Motivated Primarily by Money
questions.stem: Lena assumes her cousin launched a company purely to get rich, reasoning that a big payday is the only reason anyone starts a firm. Which myth is Lena expressing?
questions.key_rationale: Reducing entrepreneurs' motives to money alone is Myth 3. The chapter notes money is rarely the primary reason entrepreneurs start firms and persevere — founders like iRobot's Colin Angle stress missions that go beyond making money, such as changing the world in the process.

questions.focus: the ages and experience of actual business owners
questions.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Myth 4: Entrepreneurs Should Be Young and Energetic
questions.stem: A pitch competition limits entry to founders under 30, on the theory that only the young have the energy a start-up demands. Which myth underlies the rule?
questions.key_rationale: The age limit rests on Myth 4. The chapter shows business ownership spread fairly evenly across age groups, and four of the five qualities investors value in a strong entrepreneur — relevant experience, skills, a solid reputation, and a track record — favor older founders.

questions.focus: whether entrepreneurs seek public attention
questions.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Myth 5: Entrepreneurs Love the Spotlight
questions.stem: A podcast host claims that genuine entrepreneurs all crave fame, and that any founder avoiding press coverage must not be the real thing. Which myth does the host express?
questions.key_rationale: Equating entrepreneurship with craving attention is Myth 5. The chapter observes that the vast majority of entrepreneurs do not attract public attention and many avoid it — few people can name the founders of Netflix, YouTube, or DIRECTV despite using those services.

question_sets.label: The three types of start-up firms (LO 1.5)

shared_options.theme: firms that bring new products and services to market
shared_options.correction: one of the three start-up types — these firms create value by recognizing and then seizing opportunities, like Dropbox, Facebook, and Uber

shared_options.theme: firms that replace what the owner would earn in a job
shared_options.correction: one of the three start-up types — most small businesses fit here, yielding job-like income and offering common, easily available, not particularly innovative products

shared_options.theme: firms built around the owner's chosen way of living
shared_options.correction: one of the three start-up types — they let owners pursue a sport, hobby, or pastime and earn a living doing so; they are not innovative and do not grow quickly

shared_options.theme: a cautious, wait-and-see business posture
shared_options.correction: not one of the three start-up types — 'conservative' marks the low end of the entrepreneurial-intensity continuum for existing firms, not a category of start-up

shared_options.theme: entrepreneurial activity inside an established company
shared_options.correction: not one of the three start-up types — corporate entrepreneurship describes established firms behaving entrepreneurially, not a kind of independent start-up

questions.focus: a firm that replaces the income of a conventional job
questions.stem: After a decade at a salon chain, Marta opens her own hairstyling shop. It offers the same services available all over town and earns her about what her old employer paid. Which type of start-up firm is this?
questions.key_rationale: Marta's shop matches the chapter's definition of a salary-substitute firm: it yields income similar to what the owner would earn working for an employer and offers common, easily available, not particularly innovative services — hairstyling salons are among the chapter's examples.

questions.focus: a firm built around the owner's chosen way of living
questions.stem: Devon, an avid rock climber, runs a small guiding service so he can spend his days climbing and make a living from the sport he loves. He employs only himself and has no plans to grow. Which type of start-up firm is this?
questions.key_rationale: Devon's service fits the chapter's lifestyle firm: it gives the owner the opportunity to pursue a particular lifestyle — promoting a sport, hobby, or pastime — while earning a living, is not innovative, does not grow quickly, and employs only the owner or a handful of people.

questions.focus: a firm that brings something new to market
questions.stem: Two founders build a company around an app offering a service consumers couldn't get before; they spotted the opportunity and moved quickly to bring the product to market. Which type of start-up firm is this?
questions.key_rationale: This is the chapter's entrepreneurial firm: it brings new products and services to market by creating and then seizing opportunities, giving customers value they wouldn't otherwise have — the category the chapter illustrates with Dropbox, Facebook, and Uber.

source.title: Entrepreneurship: Successfully Launching New Ventures
source.authors: Bruce R. Barringer and R. Duane Ireland

learning_objectives.2.1: Explain the difference between opportunities and ideas.
learning_objectives.2.2: Describe the three general approaches entrepreneurs use to identify opportunities.
learning_objectives.2.3: Discuss the personal characteristics of entrepreneurs that contribute to their ability to recognize business opportunities.
learning_objectives.2.4: Identify and describe techniques entrepreneurs use to generate ideas.

excerpts.Chapter 2 → The Differences Between Oppo: An idea is merely a thought or notion; it may or may not qualify as an opportunity, a favorable set of circumstances creating a genuine need for a new product, service, or business. A true opportunity has four qualities: attractive, timely, durable, and anchored in something that creates value for buyers. Its window of opportunity, the period when a new firm can realistically enter the market, must still be open. Many ventures fail because no real opportunity existed.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Three Ways to Identify Oppor: Entrepreneurs use three general approaches to identify opportunities for a new venture: observing trends, solving a problem, and finding gaps in the marketplace. Understanding all three matters, because an entrepreneur who knows each approach's profile is far more likely to notice opportunities and ideas that fit one of them.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Observing Trends: The first approach to identifying opportunities is observing environmental trends; the four most important are economic forces, social forces, technological advances, and political and regulatory change. Two cautions apply: distinguish real trends from fads, since new firms rarely have the resources to exploit a fad, and remember that trends intertwine — a product like the smartphone succeeds because several trends converge. Each category, studied carefully, points to gaps between what's available and what's possible.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Solving a Problem: The second approach is recognizing a problem and building a business around its solution. Problems surface by observing the challenges people encounter in daily life, or through intuition, serendipity, or chance; many founders first experienced the problem themselves, like the inventor of the insulating coffee-cup sleeve. Technology can create problems of its own for users it doesn't fit, such as seniors struggling with cell phones. Social ventures, for-profit or nonprofit, apply this approach to problems like poverty and hunger.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Finding Gaps in the Marketpl: Marketplace gaps are the third source of opportunities: products or services people want that aren't available locally or at all. Big-box retailers compete on price with mainstream merchandise, leaving room for boutiques, specialty shops, and e-commerce sites that serve narrower needs. Gaps are often spotted when a frustrated shopper realizes others share the same unmet need — as with plus-size fashion or guitars designed for women. A gap alone isn't enough; it must still be built into a successful business.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Prior Industry Experience: Studies show prior experience in an industry helps entrepreneurs recognize opportunities: working inside it, a person may spot an underserved niche and build a network of contacts whose insights can lead to ideas. Experience also lends credibility with investors, customers, and partners. Yet it is not strictly required — outsiders like the founders of Uber and Tesla sometimes innovate precisely because fresh eyes aren't locked into an industry's traditional ways of doing things.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Cognitive Factors: Some believe entrepreneurs possess a sixth sense, entrepreneurial alertness — noticing things without deliberately searching for them. Alertness is largely a learned skill: the more knowledge someone has of an area, the more alert they tend to be to opportunities within it. Research is mixed, though; some scholars argue alertness involves purposeful effort, and that opportunity finders differ from nonfinders mainly in how well they size up the marketplace and infer its implications.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Social Networks: The breadth and depth of a person's social network affects opportunity recognition: research consistently finds that 40 to 50 percent of founders got their business idea through social contacts. The key distinction is strong versus weak ties. Strong-tie relationships — coworkers, friends, spouses — involve frequent interaction between like-minded people, so they tend to reinforce ideas a person already holds. Weak ties, the infrequent contacts with casual acquaintances, are more likely to spark a genuinely new business idea.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Creativity: Creativity — generating a novel or useful idea — underlies much opportunity recognition, and for an individual it unfolds in five stages: preparation (the background, experience, and knowledge brought to the process), incubation (mulling the problem over, consciously or not), insight (the eureka flash when the idea is born), evaluation (scrutinizing the idea's viability — a step many entrepreneurs mistakenly skip), and elaboration (working out the details into final form, such as a business plan). When stuck, return to preparation.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Brainstorming: Brainstorming is simply generating many ideas about a specific topic, from solo list-making to formal moderated group sessions. A productive formal session is freewheeling and fast-paced, and it is for generating ideas only — analysis and decisions come later. Four strict rules govern it: no criticism of any kind (even skeptical facial expressions), freewheeling is encouraged since wild ideas can lead to good ones, the pace stays quick, and leapfrogging from one idea to the next is welcomed.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Focus Groups: A focus group gathers 5 to 10 people chosen for their connection to the issue at hand — for example, a coffee shop's frequent customers. Through the give-and-take of group discussion, guided by a trained moderator who keeps things focused and lively, participants can surface ideas for new products or businesses. Focus groups work best as a follow-up to brainstorming: once a general business idea exists, the group helps refine it.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Library and Internet Researc: Library and Internet research is a third idea-generation technique. Choosing an idea first and only then researching it is too linear; the best ideas usually emerge when a general notion is combined with extensive research that sharpens it. Libraries are underused — reference librarians can point to trade journals, industry reports, and costly databases the library provides at no charge. Online, searching for new-business-idea articles, setting keyword e-mail alerts, and following industry experts on social media all feed the process.
excerpts.Chapter 2 → Other Techniques: Beyond brainstorming, focus groups, and research, firms generate ideas in other ways. Some establish customer advisory boards that meet regularly to discuss customers' needs, wants, and problems, which can point toward new ideas. Others conduct forms of anthropological research such as day-in-the-life research: Intuit, for example, routinely sends teams to users' homes and businesses to watch its products in actual use and gather insights for new product ideas.

items.stem: According to the chapter, an opportunity is best defined as:
options: a favorable set of circumstances that creates a need for a new product, service, or business
a promising thought, impression, or notion about a possible new product, service, or business
the period of time during which a firm can realistically enter a newly established market
a currently available product or service that a founder improves and builds a business around
rationales: Correct — the chapter defines an opportunity as a favorable set of circumstances that creates a need for a new product, service, or business.
A thought, an impression, or a notion is the chapter's definition of an idea — and an idea may or may not meet the criteria of an opportunity.
This describes the window of opportunity, the chapter's metaphor for when a firm can realistically enter a new market — not the opportunity itself.
The chapter calls building a business around a slightly better version of a product you like a common mistake; the key is identifying what people need and will buy, not what a founder wants to make.
probes: The chapter separates a mere thought or notion from something more — which of its two key terms does 'a thought, an impression, or a notion' actually define?
Is the definition you picked about the circumstances that create demand, or about the time period a firm has to act on them?
Does the chapter say opportunity recognition starts from a product the founder already likes, or from something else?

items.stem: According to the chapter, an idea is:
options: a thought, an impression, or a notion, which may or may not meet the criteria of an opportunity
a favorable set of circumstances that creates a need for a new product, service, or business
a plan for a new product or service that has already been shown to fill a need people will pay for
a proposal for a new product or service that becomes an opportunity once enough work is put in
rationales: Correct — an idea is a thought, an impression, or a notion, and it may or may not meet the criteria of an opportunity.
This is the chapter's definition of an opportunity, the stronger of the two terms — an idea is only a thought, an impression, or a notion.
Something already shown to fill a need people will pay for is well past a mere idea — the chapter's point is precisely that an idea may never clear that bar.
The chapter says the opposite: many ventures fail despite hard work because the idea never met the criteria of an opportunity — effort does not convert one into the other.
probes: You've picked the chapter's definition of a different term — which one describes circumstances that create demand?
If a plan has already been shown to satisfy what people need and will buy, is that still just an idea in the chapter's terms?
Does the chapter say effort turns an idea into an opportunity, or that an idea either meets the criteria of an opportunity or it doesn't?

items.stem: The chapter says an opportunity has four essential qualities. It is attractive, timely, durable, and:
options: anchored in a product, service, or business that creates or adds value for its buyer or end user
backed by a founder who is deeply passionate about the product or service being brought to market
built on a noticeable improvement to a product or service that is already selling successfully
located in a market that is established enough to prove that buyers exist for the new offering
rationales: Correct — the fourth quality is that the opportunity is anchored in a product, service, or business that creates or adds value for its buyer or end user.
Founder passion is not one of the four qualities — the chapter in fact warns against picking a business because the founder loves the product; the test is value for the buyer.
The chapter treats a slightly better version of an existing product as a common opportunity-recognition mistake, not as a defining quality of an opportunity.
Market maturity belongs to the window-of-opportunity discussion — and a maturing market is one whose window is closing, not a quality that defines the opportunity itself.
probes: The fourth quality is about who receives value from the product — the founder, or the buyer and end user?
Does the chapter present 'a better version of something already available' as a hallmark of opportunity, or as a trap?
Think of Figure 2.1 — is the fourth quality about the state of the market, or about the value the offering creates for someone?

items.stem: As the chapter uses the metaphor, a 'window of opportunity' refers to:
options: the time period in which a firm can realistically enter a new market
the moment when an entrepreneur first recognizes a problem or an opportunity gap
the shortfall between what buyers currently want and what existing firms offer them
the stretch of time a new firm needs to turn its first product version into sales
rationales: Correct — the window of opportunity is a metaphor for the time period in which a firm can realistically enter a new market: it opens once the market is established and closes as the market matures.
Recognizing a problem or gap is how internally stimulated ventures begin — the window is a property of the market's life cycle, not of the founder's moment of insight.
An unmet want is closer to an opportunity gap; the window is a time period in a market's life, not a shortfall in what firms offer.
The window measures when a market can realistically be entered, not how long a firm's own product development takes.
probes: Is the window a feature of the founder's insight, or of the market's life cycle?
The metaphor is about time — what interval opens when a market is established and closes when it matures?
Whose clock does the window run on — the firm's development schedule, or the market's growth and maturity?

items.stem: According to the chapter, a new venture is externally stimulated when the entrepreneur:
options: decides to launch a firm, searches for and recognizes an opportunity, and then starts a business
recognizes a problem or an opportunity gap and creates a business to address or fill that gap
starts a firm in response to an outside event, such as losing a job or an unexpected windfall
builds a business around an improved version of a product that other firms already sell well
rationales: Correct — in an externally stimulated start the decision to launch comes first and the search for an opportunity follows, as when Jeff Bezos set out for Seattle planning to find an attractive e-commerce opportunity.
This is the chapter's definition of an internally stimulated venture — the problem or gap is recognized first, and the business is created to address it, as with Wiivv's ill-fitting shoes.
'External' refers to where the opportunity comes from — found through an outward search — not to an outside event pushing someone toward starting a company.
The chapter presents the slightly-better-version approach as a common opportunity-recognition mistake, not as one of the two ways ventures are started.
probes: Which comes first in the externally stimulated case — the decision to launch a firm, or the recognition of a problem?
Is 'externally stimulated' about what pushed the person to become an entrepreneur, or about how the opportunity itself was found?
Does the chapter list 'improve an existing product' as one of the two ways ventures start, or as a mistake to avoid?

items.stem: The chapter traces the Internet search engine market from Yahoo's launch in 1995 through Google's entry in 1998 to Bing's recent gains. What does this example illustrate about the window of opportunity?
options: once a market matures, entering it demands compelling advantages or an exceptionally served niche
the firm that first establishes a market generally keeps the largest share after the window closes
a window of opportunity reopens whenever a competitor brings noticeably better technology along
a firm with enough resources can enter a market at any stage without regard to the window
rationales: Correct — once the search market matured, the window became less prominent: the chapter says a new entrant would now need compelling advantages over established competitors or an exemplary niche focus, and even Bing's gains took an enormous head-to-head effort by Microsoft.
Yahoo established the market and moved first, yet Google holds roughly three times Bing's share today — being first did not lock in leadership once the window closed.
Google's advanced technology succeeded because the window was still open in 1998; the chapter describes the window as closing when the market matures, not reopening with each better product.
Microsoft's experience shows the opposite — even enormous resources produced only gradual gains once the market had matured and the window had largely closed.
probes: Which firm appeared first in the example, and which firm dominates the market today?
According to the chapter, what happens to the window as a market matures — and did Google enter before or after that point?
What did it cost Microsoft to win even a fifth of the market after maturity — does that suggest the window no longer matters?

items.stem: Nadia has dreamed of being her own boss since college. This spring she quit her accounting job, spent six months studying industries and interviewing shoppers to find a customer group no one was serving well, and then launched a meal-delivery service for seniors based on what she found. Omar never planned to own a company, but after a third storm backed water into his basement he built a cheap sensor that gives early warning of flooding, and he founded a firm to sell it once he saw how many homeowners deal with the same headache. In the chapter's terms, how was each venture started?
options: Nadia's venture was externally stimulated; Omar's was internally stimulated
Nadia's venture was internally stimulated; Omar's was externally stimulated
Both ventures were externally stimulated
Both ventures were internally stimulated
rationales: Correct — Nadia decided to launch a firm first and then searched for an opportunity, the externally stimulated path; Omar first ran into a problem of his own and created a business to address it, the internally stimulated path.

This inverts the chapter's distinction by keying on motivation. Nadia's drive came from within, but the label follows where the opportunity came from: she found hers through an outward search (external), while Omar's grew out of a problem he himself experienced (internal).
Omar's firm did not begin with a decision to launch followed by a search for something worth building — it began with a problem he ran into, which is the internally stimulated pattern.
Nadia did not build her firm around a problem she had experienced — she resolved to start a company first and went looking for something worth doing, which the chapter calls externally stimulated.
probes: You may be keying on where the push came from — Nadia's inner ambition, the storm that hit Omar from outside. But the labels track how the opportunity was found, not what motivated the founder: did the person decide to launch and then go searching, or did a problem surface first and the business follow?
Rewind Omar's story to its first step. Was it a decision to start a company, or a flooded basement?
Rewind Nadia's story to its first step. Did a problem in her own life come first, or the decision to run her own company?

items.stem: Diego, a touring cellist, opened his case after a rough connecting flight to find his cello's neck cracked. Unable to find a flight case he trusted, he designed a crush-resistant one for himself, and requests from other musicians persuaded him to start a company selling it. Meanwhile, Hana's city cut trash collection to every other week, leaving her bins overflowing; she welded a compacting insert for her own cans and later founded a firm to sell the design to frustrated households. In the chapter's terms, how was each venture started?
options: Both ventures were internally stimulated
Both ventures were externally stimulated
Diego's venture was internally stimulated; Hana's was externally stimulated
Diego's venture was externally stimulated; Hana's was internally stimulated
rationales: Correct — each founder first ran into a problem in their own life (a damaged cello, overflowing bins) and then created a business to address it. Problem first, firm second is the chapter's internally stimulated pattern, the way Wiivv was started.

The airline mishap and the city's schedule change are outside events, but that is not what the labels track. Neither founder decided to launch a company and then went hunting for something to build — each solved a problem they personally experienced, so both ventures are internally stimulated.
Hana followed the same sequence as Diego — her own overflowing bins came first and the company came after — so her venture is internally stimulated too.
Diego did not set out to start a company and then search for an opening; the cracked cello came first and the business grew out of solving it, which is the internally stimulated pattern.
probes: You may be keying on the outside forces in each story — the airline, the city's new schedule. But the chapter's labels track how the opportunity was found, not where the disruption came from: did either founder decide to start a company first and then search for an opening, or did each build a business out of a problem they had already run into?
Compare Hana's first step with Diego's. Did either of them resolve to start a company before anything went wrong?
What came first for Diego — the ambition to run a company, or the cracked cello?

items.stem: According to the chapter, which of the following lists the three general approaches entrepreneurs use to identify opportunities?
options: conducting market research, interviewing customers, and analyzing competitors
brainstorming new ideas, building prototypes, and testing them with early users
observing trends, solving a problem, and finding gaps in the marketplace
following fads, licensing new technologies, and copying successful firms
rationales: Market research and competitor analysis can support any approach, but the chapter's three approaches to identifying opportunities are observing trends, solving a problem, and finding gaps in the marketplace.
Brainstorming and prototyping come after an opportunity has been identified; the chapter's three approaches are observing trends, solving a problem, and finding gaps in the marketplace.
Correct — the chapter names observing trends, solving a problem, and finding gaps in the marketplace as the three approaches entrepreneurs use to identify an opportunity a new venture can pursue.
The chapter cautions against fads — new businesses usually cannot ramp up fast enough to profit from them — and none of these three is one of its approaches to identifying opportunities.
probes: Are researching a market and studying rivals what the chapter names as ways opportunities are identified, or general business activities?
Does the chapter's list describe how ideas get developed, or three ways an opportunity is first identified?
How does the chapter say fads relate to sound opportunities — are they something new firms can usually exploit?

items.stem: When observing environmental trends to spot business opportunities, which trends does the chapter say are the most important to follow?
options: economic trends, social trends, technological advances, and political and regulatory changes
consumer confidence, housing starts, interest rates, and international exchange rates
demographic shifts, generational values, fashion cycles, and changes in popular culture
industry growth rates, venture funding levels, competitor strategies, and firm survival rates
rationales: Correct — the chapter identifies economic trends, social trends, technological advances, and political action and regulatory changes as the most important trends to follow.
Consumer spending, housing starts, and interest rates are all examples of economic forces alone — just one of the four categories of trends the chapter says to follow.
Demographic changes and cultural shifts are all examples of social forces alone — just one of the four categories of trends the chapter says to follow.
The chapter's four categories are features of the broad environment — economic, social, technological, and political and regulatory — not statistics about start-up and competitor activity.
probes: Housing starts and interest rates all belong to a single one of the chapter's categories — which other categories does it name?
Demographic change belongs to a single one of the chapter's categories — which other categories does it name?
Do the chapter's four categories describe start-up activity itself, or broader forces in the environment?

items.stem: According to the chapter, why do new businesses typically fail to benefit from a fad?
options: fads appeal mainly to consumers whose personal incomes are falling
large retailers capture fad-driven demand before start-ups can enter
fads are interconnected with other trends and therefore too complex to analyze
they lack the resources to ramp up fast enough to take advantage of it
rationales: The chapter links falling incomes to money-saving products and services, not to fads; its caution about fads concerns how quickly a new firm can scale.
The chapter says large retailers focus on popular mainstream items, leaving gaps — it does not say they absorb fad demand; its point about fads is that new firms cannot ramp up quickly enough.
Interconnection is the chapter's point about genuine trends, which should be considered together; its caution about fads is about a new firm's limited resources.
Correct — the chapter says new businesses typically do not have the resources to ramp up fast enough to take advantage of a fad, which is why trends must be distinguished from fads.
probes: Where does the chapter discuss falling incomes — in its caution about fads, or as an economic force pointing to money-saving businesses?
Does the chapter's caution about fads involve what large retailers do, or what new firms lack?
Which does the chapter describe as interconnected and worth considering together — fads, or genuine environmental trends?

items.stem: According to the chapter, how do large retailers such as Walmart and Costco help create gaps in the marketplace?
options: they locate only near large cities, leaving smaller communities with no stores
they compete mainly on price and stock popular items aimed at mainstream buyers
they undercut specialty shops on price until those local competitors close down
they rotate merchandise so quickly that many product lines never stay in stock
rationales: The chapter's point is about what large retailers choose to carry, not where they locate — their focus on high-volume mainstream items leaves niches unserved.

Correct — because these retailers compete primarily on price and carry the most popular items targeted at mainstream consumers, merchandise that sells in smaller quantities is left to clothing boutiques, specialty shops, and e-commerce websites.
The chapter presents specialty shops as beneficiaries of the gaps large retailers leave, not as victims of their pricing.
The chapter attributes gaps to what large retailers decline to carry — lower-volume merchandise — not to fast merchandise rotation.
probes: Is the chapter's explanation about the locations of big retailers, or about which merchandise they choose to carry?
In the chapter, do specialty shops lose to big retailers' prices, or thrive on what big retailers ignore?
What does the chapter say big retailers decline to carry, and why does that leave room for other businesses?
